full_judgment:
Saifuddin Ahmed Siddique was the owner of the land measuring 47.47 acres. He entered into an agreement with the writ petitioners on 28-11-1969 for sale of that land for a consideration of Taka 41,500. As the vendor failed to execute the deed of sale, the petitioners filed Other Suit No. 14 of 1981 for specific performance of contract. Ultimately, the suit was decreed by the judgment and decree dated 2-5-2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 5380 of 1991. Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1072 of 2006 filed by the heirs of the vendor was dismissed by the Appellate Division on 3.2.2007 on the ground of limitation. Soon afterwards, the petitioners put the decree in execution in Other Execution Case No. 2 of 2006. The deed of sale was executed by the Executing Court on 30-4-2008 on behalf of the vendor and it was sent to the Registrar for registration. But the Registrar refused registration of the deed of sale as stamp duty had been paid on the consideration mentioned in the agreement for sale. The Registrar claimed payment of duties on the basis of market value of the property on the date of presentation of the deed before him, prescribed by the Shammpattir Bazar Mullya Nirdharan Bidhimala, 2002 (in short, Bidhimala) as amended to date by the order dated 16-6-2008. The Executing Court asked the petitioners to comply with the demand of the Registrar and to pay stamp duty on the market value existing on the date of presentation of the deed for registration. 

 11. When the aforesaid provision was not there, a deed of sale was valued on the value as mentioned in the decree and the amount mentioned in the decree used to be the amount mentioned in the contract for the enforcement of which the decree was passed. Now that the rule requires payment on the market value on the date of presentation of the deed of sale even though the decree mentioned a lower amount, it may create, as in the present case, serious hardship. In his book, the Administrative Law, 8th Edition at pages 850 and 860, Wade has in essence, said that a rule which creates serious hardship shall have to be declared void on ground of lacking in reasonableness. Article 31 of our Constitution contains the element, due process, which requires a law to be reasonable. Thus, if the aforesaid rule is unreasonably harsh, it will be void on account of it being unreasonable and harsh. 

 12. It is a cardinal principle of interpretation that when two interpretations are possible, that interpretation has to be adopted which will avoid hardship or unjust and unreasonable result as has been held in the cases of Abdul Mutaleb vs Rezia Begum PLD 1970 SC 185 and Md Nazimuddin vs State, 30 DLR 49. "Not only are unreasonable or artificial or anomalous constructions to be avoided: it appears to be an assumption (often unspoken) of the courts that where two possible constructions present themselves, the more reasonable one is to be chosen," Maxwell-Interpretation of Statutes, 12th Edition at page 203. 

 13. The contract in the instant case was made in 1969 and the vendor did not execute and register the kabala compelling the writ petitioners to file a suit for specific performance which was contested by the vendor and also the Government. The writ petitioners were in no way responsible for the delay at least from 1979, but the writ petitioners are required to pay duties and taxes on the market value of the property on the date of presentation of the deed of sale by the Court. It seems that the Rules have been framed to avoid under valuation. In the case of contested decree of specific performance, the question of undervaluation cannot arise. Then the law should not be interpreted in a way which is not necessary to achieve the object of the legislation. If we interpret the proviso making it applicable in respect of decree of specific performance passed after the insertion of the proviso, it achieves that object of the legislation and also avoids an unjust result. According to Maxwell, "where possible, a construction should be adopted which will facilitate the smooth working of the scheme of the legislation" Interpretation of Statutes, 12th Edition at page 201. 

 14. Again, if we interpret the proviso as being applicable in respect of decree of specific performance, the rule is given retrospective effect so as to apply to events occurring before the insertion of the proviso. Principle of interpretation requires every substantive provision to be prospective unless it is made retrospective by clear words and by necessary implication In case of Rules' it cannot be given retrospective effect even by clear words if the parent law by specific language permits the delegate to give retrospective effect to the Rules as has been held in the case of Commercial Bank Ltd vs Rahimafroz Batteries 7 BLC (AD) 73. Here neither section 63A nor section 69 of the Registration Act has given power to the Government to give any provision of the aforesaid Bidhimala retrospective operation. Thus the proviso must be construed as being prospective in operation and it must be held that the instant case does not come within the mischief of the aforesaid proviso to Bidhi 5(4). 

 15. The findings and decision of this case will have no bearing on the Other Class Suit No. 533 of 2006 for declaration of title pending in the 3rd Court of Joint District Judge Chittagong.
